title: The simulation of the Antarctic ozone hole by chemistry-climate models
abstract: Abstract. While chemistry-climate models are able to reproduce many characteristics of the global total column ozone field and its long-term evolution, they have fared less well in simulating the commonly used diagnostic of the area of the Antarctic ozone hole i.e. the area within the 220 Dobson Unit (DU) contour. Two possible reasons for this are: (1) the underlying Global Climate Model (GCM) does not correctly simulate the size of the polar vortex, and (2) the stratospheric chemistry scheme incorporated into the GCM, and/or the model dynamics, results in systematic biases in the total column ozone fields such that the 220 DU contour is no longer appropriate for delineating the edge of the ozone hole. Both causes are examined here with a view to developing ozone hole area diagnostics that better suit measurement-model inter-comparisons. The interplay between the shape of the meridional mixing barrier at the edge of the vortex and the meridional gradients in total column ozone across the vortex edge is investigated in measurements and in 5 chemistry-climate models (CCMs). Analysis of the simulation of the polar vortex in the CCMs shows that the first of the two possible causes does play a role in some models. This in turn affects the ability of the models to simulate the large observed meridional gradients in total column ozone. The second of the two causes also strongly affects the ability of the CCMs to track the observed size of the ozone hole. It is shown that by applying a common algorithm to the CCMs for selecting a delineating threshold unique to each model, a more appropriate diagnostic of ozone hole area can be generated that shows better agreement with that derived from observations.
problem: Chemistry-climate models poorly simulate the Antarctic ozone hole area because systematic biases in total column ozone and incorrect simulation of the polar vortex size make the standard 220 DU contour definition inappropriate for evaluating model performance.
method: To improve inaccurate simulations of the Antarctic ozone hole, the paper proposes two model-specific methods for defining its area, using thresholds based on either the maximum meridional ozone gradient or the inner polar vortex edge, which corrects for model biases and improves agreement with observations.
task: The task is to analyze why chemistry-climate models inaccurately simulate the Antarctic ozone hole and to develop improved diagnostics that account for model biases, enabling more consistent comparisons between simulations and observations.
innovation: This paper develops alternative diagnostics for the Antarctic ozone hole area, using model-specific thresholds based on ozone gradients and the polar vortex edge, to overcome model biases and improve comparisons between chemistry-climate model simulations and observations compared to the standard 220 DU definition.

E39C-A (Stenke et al., 2008, 2009) is an upgraded version of the CCM E39C (Dameris et al., 2005, 2006) employing the fully Lagrangian advection scheme ATTILA (Reithmeier and Sausen, 2002) for tracer transport.

E39C-A (Stenke et al., 2008, 2009) is an upgraded version of the CCM E39C (Dameris et al., 2005, 2006) employing the fully Lagrangian advection scheme ATTILA (Reithmeier and Sausen, 2002) for tracer transport. ATTILA is strictly mass conserving and numerically non-diffusive.

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: semi-Lagrangian advection scheme of Williamson and Rasch (1994)
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Water vapor, cloud water and chemical trace species are advected by ATTILA instead of the operational semi-Lagrangian advection scheme of Williamson and Rasch (1994) which has been used in the previous model version E39C.

The data-base combines satellite-based ozone measurements from four Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer (TOMS) instruments, three different retrievals from the Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment (GOME) instruments, data from four Solar Backscatter Ultra-Violet (SBUV) instruments and data from the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI).
